Pointers

A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. The unary operator & returns the address of its operand, and the unary operator * dereferences a pointer, giving access to the value stored at that address.

A pointer that does not point to any valid object should be set to NULL. Dereferencing a NULL pointer is undefined behaviour.

Dynamic allocation with malloc

The function malloc, declared in stdlib.h, allocates a block of memory of the requested size in bytes on the heap and returns a pointer to the start of that block. If the allocation fails, malloc returns NULL, so the return value must always be checked before use.

Memory returned by malloc is not initialised. The function calloc allocates memory for an array and sets all of its bytes to zero.

Releasing memory with free

Every block allocated with malloc or calloc must be released with free when it is no longer needed. Memory that is allocated but never freed is called a memory leak.

After free is called, the pointer still holds the old address and is called a dangling pointer. Using a dangling pointer, or calling free twice on the same block, is undefined behaviour.
